warmup.q: Amazon built Dynamo for the shopping cart. During a network failure, two replicas end up with different versions of the same cart. What did Dynamo's designers choose to do?
options: Reject the second write, so a cart can never be in conflict
Keep both versions and let the cart service merge them when it reads
Let the version with the newest wall-clock timestamp win, always
Lock the cart on every replica before each write
warmup.why: Dynamo is "always writeable": it never refuses a write because of a failure. Conflicting versions are kept, tracked with vector clocks, and handed to the application to merge, so an added item is never lost. The price is that a deleted item can come back. Locking every replica would make writes wait on failed nodes, and timestamp-wins would silently drop one customer's change.

sections.h: One machine runs out, and splitting the data raises two questions
sections.html:
Start with a payments table on one database server. Every insert, from every instance of every service, lands on that one machine. Say your Oracle primary handles 8,000 payment inserts a second at 70% CPU, and the Black Friday forecast says 25,000.

The first fix is a bigger machine. That's called scaling up, and for most systems it's the right call. It runs out in two ways. There is a biggest machine you can buy. And it is still one machine: while it fails over to a standby (a second machine kept up to date to take over), every authorization waits.

The second fix is to split the data over several machines, each holding one part. That's scaling out, and each part is called a partition (some products say shard). For example, accounts A-0000 to A-4999 live on one server and A-5000 to A-9999 on another. Each server now takes about half the writes, and adding servers adds capacity.

Splitting raises two questions that one machine never had.

Which machine holds a given key? Every read and every write must answer this before it can do anything else. If the answer comes from one central lookup table, that table becomes the new bottleneck.

What happens when a machine dies? With 100 servers, a failed machine is a normal day, not an incident. If a key lives on only one machine, it's unreachable until that machine returns. So each key needs copies, called replicas, on other machines. Copies bring their own question: which copy is right when they disagree?

Splitting also makes some old habits expensive. A transfer between two accounts on two servers needs both servers to agree over the network. A round trip takes about 0.5 ms inside one data centre and about 70 ms between regions, and if one server is down the transfer waits. A join across servers ships rows between machines. So the first systems built to scale out left joins and multi-key transactions out.

Google and Amazon published the two answers most NoSQL stores still use. Google's Bigtable paper (OSDI 2006) keeps all keys sorted and cuts the sorted list into ranges, one server per range. When a server dies, its ranges move to another server. Bigtable ran web indexing, Google Earth and Google Finance. Amazon's Dynamo paper (SOSP 2007) hashes each key onto a ring and keeps live copies of every key on several machines, so a write never waits for a dead one. Dynamo ran the shopping cart. That is the picture for this whole lesson: sort and cut into ranges, or hash onto a ring. The figure shows both, and every store in this track uses one, the other, or a mix.

The label NoSQL came later. What the family shares is a data model that isn't relational tables, and a design that spreads data over many machines.

sections.h: Bigtable: keep the keys sorted, then cut them into ranges
sections.html:
Take one question, "show merchant M-0042's payments from today", over a table of 2 billion payments. Build a store that answers it cheaply, one version at a time.

Version 1 is a hash map from key to value, like Java's HashMap. It finds one key fast. But a hash map keeps its keys in no useful order, so "every key that starts with M-0042" means visiting all 2 billion entries.

Version 2 keeps the keys sorted, like Java's TreeMap. Sorted here means lexicographic order: compare two keys character by character, the way a dictionary orders words. Now design the key so the question becomes a prefix. In M-0042#2026-11-07T08:15:03#pay-81701, the merchant comes first, then the time, then the payment id. All of M-0042's payments sit next to each other in time order, and one day is one unbroken run. To read it, the store jumps to the first key at or after M-0042#2026-11-07 and walks forward until a key stops matching. That walk is a range read. Its cost depends on how many rows it returns, not on the size of the table. Put the payment id first and the same question visits every row again. The row key decides which questions are cheap.

Version 3 spreads the sorted list over machines. Cut it into contiguous pieces of about 100 to 200 MB; Bigtable calls a piece a tablet, and each tablet server serves many tablets. Because the pieces follow key order, a range read touches one tablet, or two when it crosses a boundary. When a tablet grows too big, its server splits it in two. The tablet files themselves live in GFS, Google's distributed file system, so when a server dies, the master (one coordinating server) assigns its tablets to other servers and they load them from GFS.

Version 4 gives the value some structure. With one opaque blob per key, changing a payment's status means rewriting the whole payment, and the old status is gone. So Bigtable addresses a value by three things. The paper writes it in one line:

(row:string, column:string, time:int64) -> string

A column name has two parts, family:qualifier, such as pay:status or risk:score. You declare families up front. Qualifiers are free, and a row stores only the columns it actually wrote: a missing column costs nothing, not even a NULL. That's what the paper means by sparse. Each cell keeps several versions under 64-bit timestamps, newest first, and a per-family setting keeps only the last n versions or only recent ones.

One rule limits what you can build on top: every read or write under a single row key is atomic (it happens completely or not at all, and no reader sees half of it), however many columns it touches. Nothing is atomic across rows.

How does a server insert into a sorted structure fast? It appends each write to a commit log, a file on disk that only grows, so the write survives a crash. Then it adds the write to a sorted buffer in memory, the memtable. A full memtable is written out as an immutable sorted file, an SSTable, and background compactions merge SSTables. That design is the LSM tree (log-structured merge tree), which lesson 5 of the database internals track builds. HBase, Google Cloud Bigtable and Cassandra all store data this way.

try.title: See the sort order a row key gives you
steps: Read SortedRowsDemo.kt below. It puts six payment rows into a TreeMap, the way Bigtable keeps rows, in the order they arrived.
Before you run it, write down the order you expect, and which rows a read of prefix M-0042#2026-11-07 returns.
Run it from the labs folder. Then explain the last two lines: why does acct#10 come before acct#9?

code.title: SortedRowsDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.nosql.l01.demo import java.util.TreeMap import java.util.TreeSet /** Bigtable keeps rows sorted by key. See what that order looks like, and what a prefix read returns. */ fun main() { // row key = merchant # time # payment id, written in the order the payments arrived val rows = TreeMap<String, String>() rows["M-0042#2026-11-07T10:30:12#pay-81730"] = "4250 EUR" rows["M-0043#2026-11-07T08:01:44#pay-81690"] = "1200 EUR" rows["M-0042#2026-11-06T23:59:58#pay-81655"] = "999 EUR" rows["M-0042#2026-11-07T08:15:03#pay-81701"] = "18000 EUR" rows["M-0041#2026-11-07T09:12:00#pay-81712"] = "450 EUR" rows["M-0042#2026-11-07T09:40:27#pay-81720"] = "7300 EUR" println("All rows, in the order the map keeps them:") rows.forEach { (key, value) -> println(" $key $value") } // a range read: jump to the first key >= the prefix, walk forward, stop at the first miss val prefix = "M-0042#2026-11-07" println("Rows starting with $prefix:") rows.tailMap(prefix).entries .takeWhile { it.key.startsWith(prefix) } .forEach { println(" ${it.key} ${it.value}") } // the classic row-key bug: numbers stored as text sort as text println("Unpadded: " + TreeSet(listOf("acct#9", "acct#10", "acct#2", "acct#100"))) println("Padded: " + TreeSet(listOf(9, 10, 2, 100).map { "acct#%06d".format(it) })) }

try.expect:
All rows, in the order the map keeps them:
  M-0041#2026-11-07T09:12:00#pay-81712  450 EUR
  M-0042#2026-11-06T23:59:58#pay-81655  999 EUR
  M-0042#2026-11-07T08:15:03#pay-81701  18000 EUR
  M-0042#2026-11-07T09:40:27#pay-81720  7300 EUR
  M-0042#2026-11-07T10:30:12#pay-81730  4250 EUR
  M-0043#2026-11-07T08:01:44#pay-81690  1200 EUR
Rows starting with M-0042#2026-11-07:
  M-0042#2026-11-07T08:15:03#pay-81701  18000 EUR
  M-0042#2026-11-07T09:40:27#pay-81720  7300 EUR
  M-0042#2026-11-07T10:30:12#pay-81730  4250 EUR
Unpadded: [acct#10, acct#100, acct#2, acct#9]
Padded:   [acct#000002, acct#000009, acct#000010, acct#000100]

Insert order doesn't matter: the key alone decides the order. The prefix read returns three rows and skips the same merchant's payment from 2026-11-06, because that key doesn't start with the prefix. Numbers stored as text compare character by character, and 1 is smaller than 9, so pad them to a fixed width.

sections.h: Dynamo: hash keys onto a ring and keep writing through failures
sections.html:
Amazon's requirement was blunt: "Add to Cart" must succeed even while servers and network links fail. Amazon measured its services at the 99.9th percentile (the latency that 999 of every 1,000 requests beat), so a store that was fast on average but stalled when one server died wasn't good enough. Dynamo calls each server a node. Here is how it gets there, again one version at a time.

Version 1 puts one copy of each key on node number hash(key) mod S, where S is the number of nodes. A hash function such as MD5 turns any key into a big number that looks random, so keys spread evenly. This breaks the day you add a node. Going from 4 nodes to 5 changes the remainder for most keys. Remainders mod 4 and mod 5 repeat every 20 numbers, and only 0, 1, 2 and 3 give the same remainder for both, so a key stays put only 4 times in 20. 80% of all keys move at once.

Version 2 uses a ring. Lay every possible MD5 value around a circle. Hash each node's name to place the node on the circle, and hash each key the same way. A key belongs to the first node you meet walking clockwise from the key. Adding a node now only takes keys from one neighbour: with 5 nodes of equal share, about a fifth of the keys move instead of 80%. That trick is consistent hashing.

Version 3 adds copies, because with one copy a dead node makes its keys unreachable. The first node clockwise, the coordinator, stores the key and sends it on to the next nodes clockwise, N nodes in all. The paper calls them the key's preference list, and N is typically 3.

Version 4 stops waiting for everyone. A write that waited for all 3 copies would be as slow as the slowest node, and impossible while any one is down. So Dynamo waits for W of them, and a read asks R of them. If R + W > N, any R readers and any W writers share at least one node, so some reply carries the latest write. With N = 3 you might pick W = 2 and R = 2. These are quorums; lesson 6 of this track runs them on Cassandra.

Version 5 keeps writing when a home node is down. The write goes to the first N healthy nodes clockwise instead. The stand-in keeps the write with a hint naming the real owner and hands it over when the owner returns. The paper calls this a sloppy quorum with hinted handoff. The stepper walks through versions 2 to 5.

The price shows up next. During a failure, two writes to the same cart can land on different nodes, and the copies disagree. Dynamo doesn't pick a winner. It tags each version with a vector clock, a short list of (node, counter) pairs that records which earlier versions it has seen. A read that finds two versions where neither has seen the other returns both, and the cart service merges them. An added item is never lost; as the paper admits, a deleted item can come back.

DynamoDB is not Dynamo. It launched in 2012, and its 2022 USENIX paper says the two share most of a name and little of the architecture. A DynamoDB partition keeps its copies in several availability zones (separate data centres in one region), and the copies elect a leader with Multi-Paxos, a consensus protocol: a way for copies to agree on one leader and one order of writes (lesson 12 of the database internals track covers Raft, a close relative). Only the leader takes writes and strongly consistent reads, the reads guaranteed to see every write that has succeeded. So there are no vector clocks for your code to merge.

try.title: Place payment keys on an MD5 ring
steps: Read PreferenceListDemo.kt. It puts six nodes on a ring at the MD5 hash of their names, then finds the three nodes that store each key.
Run it. Check one line by hand: from the key's percentage, walk clockwise through the ring printout and take the next three nodes.
Before you read the last line, predict it. The coordinator of pay-81723 is down: which node stands in, and what does it keep?

code.title: PreferenceListDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.nosql.l01.demo import java.math.BigInteger import java.security.MessageDigest // Dynamo hashes keys with MD5 onto a ring of 2^128 positions private val RING: BigInteger = BigInteger.ONE.shiftLeft(128) private fun md5(text: String): BigInteger = BigInteger(1, MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5").digest(text.toByteArray())) /** Where on the ring a hash sits, as a percentage of the way round. */ private fun percent(position: BigInteger): String = "%5.1f%%".format(position.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(1000)).divide(RING).toInt() / 10.0) /** Six nodes, one token each. Which nodes store a key, and what changes when one is down. */ fun main() { // each node takes the ring position of the hash of its name val nodes = listOf("node-A", "node-B", "node-C", "node-D", "node-E", "node-F") .map { it to md5(it) } .sortedBy { it.second } println("Ring (clockwise):") nodes.forEach { (name, token) -> println(" $name at ${percent(token)}") } // walk clockwise from the key's position; skip nodes that are down fun walk(key: String, down: Set<String> = emptySet()): List<String> { val position = md5(key) val start = nodes.indexOfFirst { it.second >= position }.let { if (it < 0) 0 else it } // wrap past 100% return (nodes.indices).map { nodes[(start + it) % nodes.size].first }.filter { it !in down } } val n = 3 for (key in listOf("pay-81723", "pay-81724", "ACCT#A-1001")) { println("$key hashes to ${percent(md5(key))}: stored on ${walk(key).take(n)}") } // one node is down: the write goes to the first N HEALTHY nodes (a sloppy quorum) val key = "pay-81723" val home = walk(key).take(n) val dead = home.first() val healthy = walk(key, down = setOf(dead)).take(n) val stranger = healthy.single { it !in home } println("$dead is down. $key goes to $healthy; $stranger keeps a hint for $dead") }

try.expect:
Ring (clockwise):
  node-A at   0.1%
  node-B at  21.2%
  node-D at  26.2%
  node-C at  42.2%
  node-F at  50.3%
  node-E at  94.9%
pay-81723 hashes to  79.0%: stored on [node-E, node-A, node-B]
pay-81724 hashes to   1.8%: stored on [node-B, node-D, node-C]
ACCT#A-1001 hashes to  48.6%: stored on [node-F, node-E, node-A]
node-E is down. pay-81723 goes to [node-A, node-B, node-D]; node-D keeps a hint for node-E

You get exactly these numbers, because MD5 gives the same hash on every machine. Two keys that differ by one digit land far apart, which spreads load. Notice how uneven the nodes are: node-E owns 44.6% of the ring (everything from 50.3% to 94.9%) and node-D only 5%. Dynamo fixes that by giving each node many positions (virtual nodes), which lesson 5 of this track builds.

sections.h: The families: what you store decides what you can ask
sections.html:
Placement decides where data lives. The data model decides which questions are cheap. Build the families up from the simplest one.

Key-value is the simplest model: put(key, value) and get(key), with the value opaque to the store. Dynamo is this model, and so is Redis (it has its own track). It answers "give me this key" fast and nothing else. "All of M-0042's payments" isn't a key.

Add a sorted second part to the key and you get the wide-column model, Bigtable's: rows grouped into partitions and sorted inside them, so a contiguous run is one read. Cassandra is this track's lead store for it.

Let the store see inside the value, a JSON-like document with nested fields and arrays, and you get the document model. MongoDB can index any field and change one field inside a document.

Store the relationships themselves and you get the graph model: nodes such as accounts and devices, edges such as "uses device". Neo4j walks from a start node along edges, so "accounts within three hops of a flagged fraudster" is one query instead of three rounds of lookups.

A last group is built around one special index each: search engines (from words to documents), time-series stores (data bucketed by time) and vector stores (nearest neighbours of an embedding, a list of numbers that stands for a text or an image).

Family You store You find it by Lead store in this track
Key-value a value or a small item of attributes its key, or a sorted run inside one partition DynamoDB (Redis has its own track)
Document JSON-like documents with nested fields any field you index MongoDB 9.0
Wide-column rows in partitions, sorted inside the partition key, then a slice of the sort order Cassandra 5.0
Graph nodes and the relationships between them a start node, then a walk along edges Neo4j
Search, time-series, vector text, measurements, embeddings an inverted index, a time bucket, nearest neighbours OpenSearch, TimescaleDB, pgvector

Real stores pair a model with a placement answer. Cassandra pairs Bigtable's model and storage engine with Dynamo's ring, copies and quorums. DynamoDB pairs key-value plus a sort key with hash partitioning and a leader per partition. HBase and Google Cloud Bigtable keep the Bigtable design whole.

Two myths are worth dropping now. "NoSQL means no schema": every store here makes you declare a key, Cassandra tables have typed columns, and MongoDB 9.0 added a constraint validation level that every inserted and updated document must pass. "NoSQL means no transactions": DynamoDB transactions cover up to 100 items, MongoDB has multi-document transactions, and Cassandra 5.0 has lightweight transactions on one partition, with multi-partition ones (Accord) in the 6.0 alpha. Lesson 10 covers what they cost.

Relational still wins when the questions aren't known in advance, when reports need joins, and when an invariant spans many rows, like a ledger that must balance. A NoSQL store pays off when you know the questions, the volume outgrows one primary, and each question touches one key or one run of keys.

try.title: Sort five payment needs into families
steps: For each need, write down the family you would reach for first and the key you would look things up by. Commit to an answer before you open the expected result.

(a) Check an idempotency key in under 5 ms, 20,000 times a second. (b) Store merchant onboarding forms whose fields differ by country and change every quarter. (c) Find accounts that share a device or a phone number with a flagged fraudster, up to three hops away. (d) Keep every card authorization for 13 months and show one card's last 50, newest first. (e) Find the merchant whose name someone typed as "Nrthwind Bikes".
try.expect: (a) Key-value: DynamoDB (or Redis) keyed by the idempotency key, one lookup per check. (b) Document: MongoDB, one document per application, with a validation rule for the fields every country shares. (c) Graph: Neo4j, start at the flagged account and walk "uses device" and "uses phone" relationships. (d) Wide-column, or key-value with a sort key: partition by card, sort by time descending, read 50 from the top. (e) Search: an inverted index with fuzzy matching, such as OpenSearch. If you put (d) in Oracle, you're not wrong at small volume. The question is where one primary stops keeping up with the writes.

refs.title: Consistency Tradeoffs in Modern Distributed Database System Design (Abadi, IEEE Computer 2012, PDF)
Apache Cassandra docs: Dynamo (how Cassandra uses the paper's ideas)

analogy: Bigtable is a giant phone book. Every entry is sorted by name and the book is split into volumes, A to C, D to F, each on its own shelf. Everyone named Kools is one flip and a short read down a page. Everyone living on Main Street means reading every volume, because the book isn't sorted by street. Dynamo is a round table of clerks. Each clerk takes the folders whose numbers fall between them and the clerk on their left, and passes copies to the next two clerks round the table. When a clerk is out sick, the next one takes the folder with a sticky note saying whose it really is. The analogy breaks in two places: a phone book is printed once, while Bigtable merges new entries into its sorted files all the time, and Dynamo's clerks can briefly hold two different versions of the same folder without noticing.
world: Your authorization path in Quarkus writes to Oracle, where one primary takes every insert. Look at the idempotency check that runs before each authorization: one lookup by one key, maybe 20,000 times a second at peak, and the key is useless after a day. That is a key-value access pattern, and it's often the first table a payments team moves to DynamoDB or Redis. The ledger, with its rule that every transfer's debits and credits balance and its month-end reports, stays relational. A Kafka consumer that builds each merchant's daily payment view fits a wide-column table keyed by merchant and day. Choose per access pattern, not per company. The rest of this track builds that habit.
mistake: The most common mistake is choosing a NoSQL store for its name and then modeling it like the relational schema you already have: one table per entity, foreign keys as plain attributes, and the queries worked out later. The store has no joins and no optimizer to rescue you, so every new question becomes a full scan or a second copy of the data. People do it because the relational habit runs deep and the tables look familiar. The fix is the next lesson: write the access patterns down first, then design keys so each one is a single lookup or a single range read.

compare.title: One payment as a relational row and as Bigtable cells

a.label: Relational row
a.title: Oracle
a.html: -- the schema fixes the columns for every row CREATE TABLE payment ( payment_id VARCHAR2(20) PRIMARY KEY, merchant_id VARCHAR2(20) NOT NULL, status VARCHAR2(12) NOT NULL, amount_minor NUMBER(19) NOT NULL, risk_score NUMBER(4,2) -- NULL for most rows ); INSERT INTO payment VALUES ('pay-81701', 'M-0042', 'CAPTURED', 18000, NULL); UPDATE payment SET status = 'SETTLED' WHERE payment_id = 'pay-81701'; -- the old status is gone unless you keep a history table

b.label: Bigtable cells
b.title: row key, column, timestamp: value
b.html:
M-0042#2026-11-07T08:15:03#pay-81701  pay:amount  t=100  18000
M-0042#2026-11-07T08:15:03#pay-81701  pay:status  t=300  SETTLED
M-0042#2026-11-07T08:15:03#pay-81701  pay:status  t=200  CAPTURED

# no risk:score cell at all: nothing stored, not even a NULL
# the update added a version; reads see t=300 first
# only the row key is indexed; there is no WHERE status = ?

compare.note: The relational row has a fixed set of typed columns, keeps one current value per column, and lets you index and query any column. The Bigtable row has whatever columns it wrote, keeps several timestamped versions per cell, and can only be found by its row key or a range of row keys. That is why the row key carries the merchant and the time: in Bigtable the key is the query.

worked.title: Design a row key for "a merchant's latest payments"

steps.say: Write the question down first: show merchant M-0042's 50 most recent payments. A Bigtable-style store does two cheap things, get one row and read a range of rows in key order. So the answer has to be one range.
steps.code: access pattern: merchant = M-0042, newest first, stop after 50

steps.say: First try: the payment id as the row key. Each payment has a unique key, but one merchant's payments are scattered across the whole key space, so the question becomes a full table scan.
steps.code:
pay-81655  pay-81690  pay-81701  pay-81712  pay-81720 ...
# M-0042's rows are mixed in with every other merchant's

steps.say: Second try: merchant, then time, then payment id. Now one prefix read covers exactly M-0042's payments. But they come out oldest first, so the newest 50 sit at the end of the range, and a forward read passes every older payment to reach them.
steps.code: fun rowKey(merchantId: String, at: Instant, paymentId: String) = "$merchantId#$at#$paymentId" // oldest first within the merchant

steps.say: Third try: store the time reversed. Long.MAX_VALUE minus the epoch millis gets smaller as time moves on, so the newest payment sorts first. Pad it to 19 digits so it compares correctly as text. A prefix read of M-0042# with a limit of 50 now stops after exactly 50 rows.
steps.code: fun rowKey(merchantId: String, at: Instant, paymentId: String): String { // newest first: bigger time, smaller number val reversed = Long.MAX_VALUE - at.toEpochMilli() return "$merchantId#${"%019d".format(reversed)}#$paymentId" }

steps.say: Check the price. All of one merchant's new payments now land at the start of the same key range, which lives on one tablet. For a merchant taking thousands of payments a second, that one tablet server takes every write. Lesson 5 of this track spreads a hot key across several ranges and merges them on read.

lab.title: Build a tiny Bigtable: one sorted map of cells
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. All seven fail with NotImplementedError. No Docker needed: this lab is plain Kotlin.
Write CellKey.compareTo: row ascending, then column ascending, then timestamp descending. The first test passes.
Write put. Reject a column whose family isn't declared (familyOf is given), insert the cell, then delete every version of that cell beyond maxVersions.
Write versions. Start at CellKey(row, column, Long.MAX_VALUE) and walk forward while the row and column still match. get is built on it, so its test passes too.
Write readRow and scan the same way: jump to the first possible key, walk forward, stop at the first key that no longer matches. Run the tests until all seven pass.
hints: Why Long.MAX_VALUE? Timestamps sort in reverse, so the biggest timestamp is the smallest key of a cell. CellKey(row, "", Long.MAX_VALUE) is the first possible key of a whole row, because "" sorts before every column name.
cells.tailMap(from, true) is a live view from from to the end of the map. Walk it with .entries.asSequence().takeWhile { ... } and you never touch the rest of the table.
In readRow, compare the row with ==. Row pay-10 starts with pay-1, and the test checks that you don't pick it up. In scan, startsWith is right, because there you want the prefix.
To drop old versions in put, collect the extra keys into a list first, then remove them. Removing entries while you iterate over a view of the same map throws ConcurrentModificationException.

drill.title: A newest-first row key from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lesson. Write a Kotlin function rowKey(merchantId: String, at: Instant, paymentId: String): String whose keys make a prefix read of "$merchantId#" return that merchant's payments newest first. Then write one sentence on why the number must be padded. Compare with the answer.

answer.html: fun rowKey(merchantId: String, at: Instant, paymentId: String): String { // later time -> smaller number -> sorts first val reversed = Long.MAX_VALUE - at.toEpochMilli() // fixed width: as text, "10" sorts before "9", so every number needs the same length return "$merchantId#${"%019d".format(reversed)}#$paymentId" }

recap: Bigtable (2006) and Dynamo (2007) traded SQL, joins and multi-row transactions for spreading data over many machines and staying up when they fail.
Bigtable is one sparse map sorted by row key, cut into tablets. The row key decides where data lives and which questions are a cheap range read. Only single-row operations are atomic.
Dynamo hashes keys onto a ring of equal nodes, copies each key to N nodes, and uses R and W quorums. A sloppy quorum with hinted handoff keeps it writeable when a node is down.
Cassandra combines a Dynamo ring with Bigtable's LSM storage. DynamoDB shares Dynamo's name and hash partitioning but uses a Multi-Paxos leader per partition.
Sort stores by data model (key-value, document, wide-column, graph, specialized) and by lineage. "No schema" and "no transactions" are both out of date.

explain.prompt: A colleague says: "DynamoDB is the Dynamo paper as a service, so our code will have to merge conflicting versions with vector clocks." Explain what's right and what's wrong about that.
explain.answer: The name and one big idea carry over. DynamoDB hashes the partition key to spread items over partitions, as Dynamo hashed keys onto a ring. But DynamoDB is a different design. Its 2022 paper says it shares little of Dynamo's architecture: each partition has replicas in several availability zones that elect a leader with Multi-Paxos, and only the leader takes writes and strongly consistent reads. So a single table in one Region never hands your code two conflicting versions of an item, and there are no vector clocks to merge. Dynamo's leaderless ring, sloppy quorums and application-side merges live on in Cassandra and Riak, not in DynamoDB.

deeper.html:
Dynamo's paper has a table that maps each problem to the technique that solves it. It's the best one-page map of the distributed ideas in this track:

Problem Technique Where you meet it again
Partitioning Consistent hashing Lesson 5
Highly available writes Vector clocks, merged on read Lesson 9
Temporary failures Sloppy quorum and hinted handoff Lesson 6
Permanent failures Anti-entropy with Merkle trees Lesson 6
Membership and failure detection Gossip Lesson 6

Bigtable leans on other Google systems that the paper describes briefly. It stores its log and SSTable files in GFS, a distributed file system, so a tablet server holds no data that would be lost with its disk. It uses Chubby, a lock service whose five replicas agree using Paxos, to make sure only one master runs and to track which tablet servers are alive. When a tablet server dies, the master gives its tablets to other servers, which replay the commit log from GFS. That is a sharp contrast with Dynamo: Bigtable recovers by moving responsibility to another server, while Dynamo keeps several live copies and keeps writing.

Abadi's PACELC paper, which you'll read properly in lesson 9, classifies these systems by two trade-offs: what they give up during a network partition, and what they trade between latency and consistency the rest of the time. By that paper's 2012 labels, Dynamo and Cassandra choose availability and low latency, while Bigtable and HBase choose consistency in both cases.
